100 PRECONFERENCE: The Second Disability, Communication, and Media Preconference 2025:
Disability Research as Disruptive Research
Tuesday Pre/Postconferences
9:00–17:00
OFFSITE
EVENTS
(Offsite)
Organizers
Meryl Alper, Northeastern U, USA
Lorenzo Dalvit, Rhodes U, SOUTH AFRICA
Elizabeth Ellcessor, U of Virginia, USA

Gerard Goggin, Western Sydney U, AUSTRALIA
Beth Haller, Towson U, USA

Francis Routledge, U of Toronto, CANADA
Wenqi Tan, U of Sydney, AUSTRALIA
M. Remi Yergeau, U of Michigan, USA
Kuansong Victor Zhuang, Nanyang Technological U, SINGAPORE
A key focus of this year’s preconference is to foster a supportive community of scholars and thinkers
across disability, communication, and media research. We are building upon our inaugural preconference
at ICA 2024, where we had more than 50 attendees both online and in-person, to provide a space for
collaboration, conversation, and mentorship.
The disability, communication, and media preconference will be a hybrid event. It will consist of:
1) A postgraduate and early career researcher consortium (to be held in the morning, Mountain Time);
2) A. workshop with expert speakers and senior scholars in disability, communication, and media studies;
and
3) A roundtable discussion on the future of the field.
1000 PRECONFERENCE: 11th
Journalism Studies Graduate Student Colloquium
Wednesday Pre/Postconferences
8:30–17:00 Journalism Studies
OFFSITE
EVENTS
(Offsite)
Organizers
Mathias Felipe de-Lima-Santos, Macquarie U, AUSTRALIA
Raul Ferrer-Conill, U of Stavanger, NORWAY
Edson Tandoc, Nanyang Technological U, SINGAPORE
The 11th
Journalism Studies Graduate Student Colloquium is an annual event dedicated to supporting the
professional growth of graduate students and early career scholars in the field of journalism studies. This
colloquium is organized as a preconference event. The colloquium is designed to foster academic
mentorship, offering graduate students a unique opportunity to present their research in a supportive,
constructive, and international environment. Participants will engage with both peers and leading scholars
to receive personalized feedback on their work, enhancing their research and contributing to their
professional development.

Wednesday Pre/Postconferences
8:00–17:00 Political Communication

Brian Ekdale, U of Iowa, USA

2
Ryan Stoldt, Drake U, USA
Bingbing Zhang, U of Iowa, USA
Organizers
Katy Biddle, U of Southern Mississippi, USA
Tim Havens, U of Iowa, USA
Andy High, Pennsylvania State U, USA
Raven Maragh-Lloyd, Washington U in St. Louis, USA
Javie Ssozi, U of Iowa, USA
This preconference aims to bring scholars together to 1) interrogate the conceptualization of radicalization
in research about social media, 2) diversify perspectives on radicalization online, 3) highlight work on
radicalization that focuses on more “mundane” and “everyday” forms of radicalization online, and 4)
considers radicalization as attitudinal or perceptual rather than solely as an outcome of a process.

Wednesday Pre/Postconferences
9:00–17:300

Journalism Studies
Mass Communication
Organizers
Mark Boukes, U of Amsterdam, NETHERLANDS
Terry Flew, U of Sydney, AUSTRALIA
Agata Stepnik, U of Sydney, AUSTRALIA
The question of trust in media is one of the major questions of our time, and communication scholarship
has long been engaged with questions of trust. This preconference focuses on the relevance of the concept
of trust to contemporary communication debates, particularly pertaining to digital societies and emergent
communication technologies.
1100 PRECONFERENCE: Frames of Transition: Visual Communication in Times of Social Change
Wednesday Pre/Postconferences
9:00–17:00
OFFSITE
EVENTS
(Offsite)
Global Communication and Social Change
Visual Communication Studies
Chair
T.J. Thomson, RMIT U, AUSTRALIA
Organizers
Kareem El Damanhoury, U of Denver, USA
Nataliia Laba, U of Groningen, NETHERLANDS
This event seeks to encourage critical reflection on the potentials and limitations of visual communication
in representing and addressing social change, promoting a nuanced understanding of (i) how visual
content can both empower and marginalize; (ii) how individuals, groups, and organizations visually
represent and engage with change; and (iii) how communication scholars can contribute to understanding
change through innovative visual methods in a period where stability has given way to provisionality
across every domain.

OFFSITE
EVENTS
(Offsite)
Organizers
Mandy Badermann, U of Tuebingen, GERMANY
Ross Dahlke, U of Wisconsin–Madison, USA
Kylie Falcione, U of California, Santa Barbara, USA
Jason Greenfield, New York U, USA
Rachael Kee, U of California, Davis, USA
Sue Lim, Michigan State U, USA
Jula Luehring, U of Vienna, AUSTRIA
Hannah Overbye-Thompson, U of California, Santa Barbara, USA
Patrick Parschan, LMU Munich, GERMANY
Fabio Votta, U of Amsterdam, NETHERLANDS
Advancing open and collaborative research practices in communication is contingent upon sharing tools,
ideas, skills, and data across subfields. Although conferences are undoubtedly beneficial for pursuing
these goals, they rarely afford the unstructured time and hands-on collaboration required to fully realize
their potential for catalyzing new connections and collaborations. Hackathons provide a collaborative,
low-risk opportunity to experiment with new ideas, find potential collaborators, and try something a little
“out of the box.”

Addressing ICA’s 75th
anniversary, the 2025 mobile communication preconference is an invitation to
critically reflect on the disruptive versus consolidating role of mobile media and mobile communication
in everyday life, as well on how mobile communication as a field has disrupted and consolidated
communication in the past and will in the future.
1100 PRECONFERENCE: Echoes and Overlaps in Arab and African Thought on Media and Culture
Wednesday Pre/Postconferences
9:00–17:00
OFFSITE
EVENTS
(Offsite)
Global Communication and Social Change
Philosophy, Theory, and Critique
Organizers
Clovis Bergere, Northwestern U in Qatar, QATAR
Nabil Echchaibi, U of Colorado Boulder, USA
Marwan Kraidy, Northwestern U in Qatar, QATAR
Jointly organized by the Center for Media, Religion and Culture at the University of Colorado Boulder
(CMRC) and the Institute for Advanced Study in the Global South at Northwestern University in Qatar
(#IAS_NUQ), this one-day preconference explores the intellectual and epistemic common grounds,
interactions, and constructive divergences in African and Arab scholarship on media and culture. More
than an invitation to talk back to the West, our endeavor is first and foremost driven by a desire to forge
new directions for media and communication research by building on long-standing—yet often
repressed—theories, methods, and literatures within the Africa and the Arab world.

2000 PRECONFERENCE: Artificial Intelligence in Journalism From a Global Perspective: Past,
Present, and Future
Thursday Pre/Postconferences
8:00–11:30 Media Industry Studies
OFFSITE
EVENTS
(Offsite)
Organizers
Maximilian Eder, LMU Munich, GERMANY
Helle Sjøvaag, U of Stavanger, NORWAYThis listing only includes educational sessions. For complete program details, including networking events, visit the
online program and/or event mobile app.
9
Location: OFF-SITE: MSU Denver, located at 900 Auraria Parkway, Denver, CO 80204
Over the past two decades, AI- and algorithm-based technologies have changed how information is
produced and moves within a news ecosystem in many countries worldwide. Against this background,
there is an urgent need to understand the past, present, and future implications of this shift toward
automation and AI-driven newswork. This preconference focuses on bringing together scholars working
on understanding and studying AI- and algorithm-based technologies concerning journalism and the media
industry.

2000 PRECONFERENCE: Research on Science Communication: Role and Contribution to
Communication Science and Beyond
Thursday Pre/Postconferences
8:00–16:00
OFFSITE
EVENTS
(Offsite)
Discussants
Bruno Takahashi, Michigan State U, USA
Sahana Udupa, LMU Munich, GERMANY
Organizers
Nils Bienzeisler, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, GERMANY
Janine Blessing, U of Zürich, SWITZERLAND
Bernhard Goodwin, LMU Munich, GERMANY
Lars Guenther, LMU Munich, GERMANY
Friederike Hendriks, Technische U Braunschweig, GERMANY
Niels Mede, U of Zurich, SWITZERLAND
Andreas Scheu, CMC Austrian Academy of Sciences/Alpen Adria U, AUSTRIA
Mike Schäfer, U of Zürich, SWITZERLAND
The preconference examines the role and contributions of research on science communication as part of
communication science. It consolidates science communication research within the international field of
communication science and reflects its relevance to the discipline’s different subfields like Journalism
Studies, Environmental Communication, Health Communication, or Communication and Technology.
Additionally, it assesses the field’s importance beyond academia; for communicators, policymakers, civil
society actors, and others, and critically reflects on its contributions to societal challenges.

2000 PRECONFERENCE: Political Communication PhD Student Preconference
Thursday Pre/Postconferences
7:30–16:30 Political Communication
OFFSITE
EVENTS
(Offsite)
Organizer
Kate Kenski, U of Arizona, USA
This preconference has three main goals: 1) Get feedback from senior colleagues and peers on your PhD
research; 2) Provide insights on important aspects of academia such how to publish, research ethics, and
building a CV; and 3) Cultivate a network among early career political communication scholars. To
achieve these goals, the preconference will bring together a select group of PhD students working on
political communication projects and provide them with the opportunity to present and discuss their
projects in a constructive atmosphere.
2008 PRECONFERENCE: Disrupting and Consolidating Human-Machine Communication
Thursday Pre/Postconferences
8:00–17:00 Human-Machine Communication
Mineral A
(Regency 3) Organizers
Marco Dehnert, U of Arkansas, USA
Katrin Etzrodt, Technische U Dresden, GERMANY
Jihyun Kim, U of Central Florida, USA
Andrew Prahl, Nanyang Technological U, SINGAPORE
Nan Wilkenfeld, U of California, Santa Barbara, USA
Kun Xu, U of Florida, USA
The HMC preconference aims to facilitate scholarly dialogues about theories, methodologies, and
empirical findings/evidence that help us better understand how machines are disrupting (1) how humans
communicate, (2) how scholars approach communication research, and (3) the nature of human
dialogue/hybrid human-machine synergy. The preconference will primarily consist of curated panels and a

This panel discusses the dynamic relations between digital platforms and journalism through the
perspective of disentangling from platform power. Papers analyze counter-power through legal
frameworks, a professional council’s role in delimiting platform power, journalists’ changing perceptions

the papers offer insights into strategies, perceptions, practices and alliances that enhance the disentangling
from platform power and contribute to enriching the dynamic concept of platform power.

civic agency in the context of datafication. Moving away from easy binaries, all papers present more
grounded realities of data-driven advocacy and civic tech with ambivalent actors aiming for change and
achieving imperfect results.

This panel takes the opportunity of ICA’s 75th
anniversary to think broadly about how the association has
changed or failed to change over time. Recognizing that associations are always wrestling with multiple
forces for development and growth, the panel brings together six scholars who came of age in ICA and
the field in three different decades of its evolution to share their reflections on what was significant or
might have been different in how the association evolved.

Amid rapid digitization, platformization, and fragmentation, the concept of “mass communication” has
become increasingly diffuse and multifaceted. Traditional notions of a unified audience have evolved into
diverse, segmented, and interactive communities; thus, prompting questions about what “mass
communication” truly means today and how to study it. This panel offers insights into the theoretical
perspectives and innovative methods that are needed for understanding and researching mass
communication in this changing landscape.

John Erni, Education U of Hong Kong, HONG KONG

Ed McLuskie, Boise State U, USA

Barbie Zelizer, U of Pennsylvania, USA

Mark Andrejevic, Monash U, AUSTRALIA

Tanja Bosch, U of Cape Town, SOUTH AFRICA
How Can PTC Overcome the Silencing of Critical and Deviant Scholarship?
Hanan Badr, U of Salzburg, AUSTRIA
Echoing Stuart Hall, this roundtable asks: In an ever more politically dangerous and divided world, has
theory left media and communication scholars off the hook? Theory holds the potential for transformation
through critique, but have media and communication scholars kept their end of the bargain? The panelists
offer their interventions by reflecting on the history of the division and its place within the ICA while
charting new possibilities for the future of the philosophy of communication, theory, and critique.

contributions of the Feminist Scholarship Division to the field of communication studies and to the ICA
organization, through short reports by some who led its development and work over the last four decades.

field’s theories and literature, its move toward intersectional analysis, its influence on methodologies, and
the numerous ways that it has reshaped the ICA organization.

3560 BLUE SKY PEDAGOGICAL WORKSHOP: Equitable Grading Practices in Communication

Katrina Hanna, California State U, Long Beach, USA

Equitable Grading Practices in Communication is a workshop focused on introducing and guiding
communication faculty on the core principles of equitable grading practices (Feldman, 2018). The three
pillars of equitable grading are that grades should be accurate, bias resistant, and motivational. The
workshop introduces participants to these pillars and how they may be applied in our discipline and has
them workshop their syllabus policies to reflect the principles of grading for equity.

3609 PARTNER PANEL: IGS - Korzybski Reconsidered in the Context of Contemporary
Communication Studies
Friday Partner Panel
16:30–17:45
Mineral B
(Regency 3)
Chair
Lance Strate, Fordham U, USA
Participant
Margaret Cassidy, Adelphi U, USA
Thom Gencarelli, Manhattan U, USA
Lance Strate, Fordham U, USA
Laura Trujillo-Liñán, U Panamericana, MEXICO
With the publication of the 6th edition of Alfred Korzybski’s Science and Sanity in 2023, followed by a
semester-long online reading group organized during fall 2024, and the publication of the 4th edition of
Korzybski’s General Semantics Seminar 1937: Olivet College Lectures in 2024, contemporary
communication scholars have had a good opportunity to reexamine the central work of the founder of
general semantics. Often overlooked in favor of more accessible writers such as S.I. Hayakawa, Wendell
Johnson, Irving Lee, and Neil Postman; sometimes denigrated for being scientistic; much of the time
dismissed for operating outside of academic circles and appealing to fringe intellectuals; and to a
significant extent forgotten as his contributions have been integrated into other systems without attribution,
a critical examination of Korzybski’s work is long overdue. Toward that end, this panel will consider the
ways in which his ideas and his non-aristotelian system have contributed to communication studies, what
contributions they yet may make for communication scholarship, and how and why they have failed to
adequately address contemporary concerns.

3731 A Half Century of Agenda-Setting Research: Honoring the Lives and Contributions of Maxwell
McCombs and Donald Shaw
Friday Sponsored Sessions
18:00–19:15
Colorado B
(Grand 2)
Journalism Studies
Mass Communication
Political Communication
Chair
David Weaver, Indiana U Bloomington, USA
Participant
Lindita Camaj, U of Florida, USA
Lei Guo, Fudan U, CHINAThis listing only includes educational sessions. For complete program details, including networking events, visit the
online program and/or event mobile app.
125
Brad Hamm, Northwestern U, USA
Thomas Johnson, U of Texas at Austin, USA
Sharon Meraz, U of Illinois at Chicago, USA
Sebastian Valenzuela, Pontificia U Católica de Chile, CHILE
Chris Vargo, U of Colorado Boulder, USA
Maxwell McCombs of the University of Texas at Austin passed away in September 2024. He is best
known for cofounding the groundbreaking agenda-setting theory of mass media effects with Donald Shaw,
a theory that has shaped how we understand the role of media in influencing public opinion. Shaw, equally
renowned for his significant contributions, passed away in 2021. This panel serves as a tribute to
McCombs and Shaw’s extraordinary legacy as both scholars and educators. It will celebrate their profound
contributions to the field and honor their intellectual impact in carrying forward the pioneering theories for
future generations of scholars. The program will feature a keynote address from McCombs and Shaw’s
close colleague and friend, David Weaver, alongside a panel of agenda-setting scholars, who will reflect
on their shared academic journey and the lasting influence of these two remarkable thinkers.
3733 Report Launch: A Better Way to Cover Hate?
Friday Satellite Events
18:00–18:45
Maroon Peak
(Grand 2)
Global Communication and Social Change
Journalism Studies
Chair
Cherian George, Hong Kong Baptist U, HONG KONG
Participants
Stewart Hoover, U of Colorado Boulder, USA
“Covering Hate Speech: A Guide for Journalists” is a new publication of UNESCO, the United Nations
Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. Its author, Cherian George, presents its key takeaways.
Although most take hate speech seriously as a problem that news media can either worsen or help mitigate,
journalists have failed to respond adequately to this challenge. Part of the reason is a tendency to fixate on
individual instances of norm-violating speech such as a politician’s remark, a celebrity’s social media post,
or an offensive cartoon. Journalists could instead cover hate the way they investigate other complex social
problems, such as corruption, trafficking, and pollution—not just as episodic violations but as systems and
networks needing to be traced and exposed. Hadiya Roderique (University of Toronto Scarborough) and
Stewart Hoover (University of Colorado Boulder) will kick off the discussion.

4081 LIVE FROM CALABAR, NIGERIA II: Whose Complaining: Subaltern Voices in a Masculinized
Social Media Landscape
Saturday Regional Hub
7:00–8:15
Online Only Chair
Obed Hailsham, Ignatius Ajuru U of Education, NIGERIA
Participant
Jake Effoduh, Toronto Metropolitan U, CANADA
As far-right politics surges globally, social media platforms are adjusting moderation policies to appease
free speech absolutists. Following Trump’s political resurgence, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced
replacing fact-checking with community notes, citing a need for “masculine energy” in tech—possibly a
dog whistle dismissing minoritized users’ complaints. This panel examines who gets framed as a
complainer, the role of AI in moderating grievances, and explores how platform governance can be
challenged to amplify subaltern voices.

4081 LIVE FROM MANIPAL-UDUPI, INDIA: Disruption and Consolidating Communication Research:
A South Asian Perspective
Saturday Regional Hub
8:30–9:45
Online Only Chair
Sanjay Bharthur, Manipal Institute of Communication, INDIAThis listing only includes educational sessions. For complete program details, including networking events, visit the
online program and/or event mobile app.
130
Participants
Kundan Aryal, Tribhuvan U, NEPAL
Abu Buniyan, U of Dhaka, BANGLADESH
Shugofa Dastgeer, Texas Christian U, USA
Rachel Jacob, Royal Thimphu College, BHUTAN
Bushra Rahman, Beaconhouse National U, PAKISTAN
The digital media surge in South Asia has redefined communication practices, fostering participatory
engagement while amplifying misinformation. Context-specific factors—like linguistic diversity, political
polarization, and caste dynamics—deeply shape both media content and communication theory.
Methodologically, researchers face challenges in accessing granular digital data, navigating platform
opacity, and adapting Western-centric theories. Despite these constraints, evolving indigenous frameworks
and mixed methods approaches offer rich opportunities for grounded, culturally resonant communication
scholarship in the region.

4110 Histories of Alternative Media Objects
Saturday Communication History
9:00–10:15
Mineral C
(Regency 3)
Chair
Jaime Kirtz, Arizona State U, USA
Participants

Jaime Kirtz, Arizona State U, USA

Rachel Plotnick, Indiana U Bloomington, USA

Nora Draper, U of New Hampshire, USA
Through focusing on overlooked communication media histories, this panel challenges conventional
historical narratives to offer a more expansive view of communication history. Participants offer critical
interventions through diverse case studies focusing on alternative histories of communication media
(decline of Polaroid, skycasting) and overlooked media artifacts (wristwatches, toilets as media furniture).

historical communication projects and media products.

4133 Productive (Un)Play: The Platformization, Financialization, and Problematization of Digital Game
Labor
Saturday Game Studies
9:00–10:15
Maroon Peak
(Grand 2)
Participants
Reflexivity in Platformized Game Production: Developer Accounts on Roblox’s Dress to Impress
Erika Solis, Penn State U, USA
Daniel Nielsen, Charles U, CZECHIA
Strategic Play: Hacking, Roaming and Mutual Aid Practices of Platform Game Workers in China
Mengyang Zhao, U of California, Santa Cruz, USA

Crypto Gamers
Jiaxi Hou, RMIT U, CHINA

Changwen Chen, Tsinghua U, CHINA
This panel traces the latest dynamics in digital game labor as games and gamified features are increasingly
intertwining with webs of production and reproduction. Five panelists explore labor practices across game
developers, game-related gig workers, and diverse players. Our discussion focuses on what defines digital
game labor as productive and how different entities extract value from and (re)shape contemporary
gameplay. Rather than confining “productive” to market or monetary dimensions, we examine the broader
social, cultural, and ideological ramifications of gaming and nongaming activities.

4140 Digital Borders: Between Exclusion and Inclusion?
Saturday Popular Media & Culture
9:00–10:15
Grays Peak A
(Grand Conv
Center 2)
Discussant
Philipp Seuferling, London School of Economics & Political Science, UNITED KINGDOM
Participants
DigiBorders: Everyday Borderwork in the Digital World
Sabina Mihelj, Loughborough U, UNITED KINGDOM
Cesar Jimenez-Martinez, London School of Economics & Political Science, UNITED KINGDOM
Streaming Platform Imaginaries: Audiences, Media Borders and Southeast Asian Streaming
Annette Hill, Jönköping U, SWEDEN
Digital Solidarity: Genealogy of a Bordering Concept
Stanislav Budnitsky, Colgate U, USA
Studies on digital borders have predominantly focused on migrants and refugees, stressing the most
explicit manifestations of borders as well as on how these are enforced by nation-states. As such, they risk
overlooking other ways in which digital borders structure everyday activities, from shopping and
entertainment to news consumption. This panel will therefore advance discussions by examining how
digital borders are reproduced in more subtle ways, as apparently invisible, ephemeral or easy to cross
structures.

4261 BLUE SKY BIG IDEAS: Consolidating Communication Research Through Causal Inference
Saturday Blue Sky Workshops
10:30–11:45
Mt. Yale
(Grand 3)
Organizers
Shuning Lu, U of Maryland, USA
Ewa Maslowska, Institute of Communications Research, USA
Harsh Taneja, U of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
Nathan Walter, Northwestern U, USA
The societal impact of communication motivated the establishment of communication studies. However,
establishing causality within the field remains challenging, especially in technologically mediated
contexts. Communication is a diverse field, and causal interpretations vary across traditions. This
workshop will explore how different subfields address causality, emphasizing the need for causal
explanations to enhance theory building. It will also discuss methodological approaches, challenges, and
future directions for establishing causality in communication research.

170
Asheley Landrum, Arizona State U, USA
David Scales, Weill Cornell Medical College, USA
Brian Southwell, RTI International, USA
Misinformation about science is not new and has been a subject of consistent and considerable attention
among communication scholars. The COVID pandemic however drew the attention of publics,
practitioners and policymakers to the topic with proposals to mitigate its perceived impact. The challenge
is that there have been multiple definitions of misinformation about science reflecting the fact that the
work has been pursued in many different disciplines making it difficult to gain a comprehensive
understanding of the research and assess its impact. The National Academy of Science, Engineering and
Medicine (NASEM) convened an expert group of scholars from different disciplines to define
misinformation about science, document the sources, understand the factors influencing the spread, and
assess its potential impact. The report also examined interventions that can mitigate the impact of
misinformation about science. This panel, composed of members of the Consensus Study Committee, will
discuss the report’s major highlights, research gaps and implications for communication scholars to
advance the science and address how misinformation about science originates, spreads and minimize its
impact. Chair: K. Viswanath, Harvard University & Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Chair of the Consensus
Study; Committee Panelists: David Scales, Weill Cornell Medical College, Committee Member; Ashley
Landrum, Arizona State University, Committee Member; Brian Southwell, RTI International, Committee
Member

4304 (HYBRID) ICA@75 ANNIVERSARY SPECIAL SESSION: Science Under Fire
Saturday Sponsored Sessions
12:00–13:15
Centennial E
(Regency 3)
Organizer
Jessica Piotrowski, U of Amsterdam, NETHERLANDS
Participants
Hanan Badr, U of Salzburg, AUSTRIA
Jiyoung Han, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, KOREA (THE REPUBLIC OF)
Dhavan Shah, U of Wisconsin–Madison, USA
Amanda Third, Western Sydney U, AUSTRALIA
Saskia Witteborn, Chinese U of Hong Kong, HONG KONG
Following up on a panel at ICA24 entitled “Scholars under Attack,” this panel broadens our discussion to
address the growing challenges faced by communication scholars as they navigate a climate of heightened
scrutiny and hostility. In today’s environment, we see that researchers are increasingly encountering the
adverse effects of misinformation, political interference, targeted harassment, and the weaponization of
government transparency acts. These pressures complicate academic work, often leading to heightened
anxiety and diminishing the freedom necessary for robust scientific inquiry. This panel brings together
experts across various domains of communication science to examine the multifaceted impact of these
challenges on scholars at different career stages. Panelists from across the globe will reflect on threats to
political communication, journalism, climate change, activism, the youth’s media space, and more. With
concrete (and sometimes harrowing) stories, the discussion aims to shed light on the lived experiences of
affected researchers, fostering a deeper understanding of the systemic issues at play. Ultimately, the panel
aims to identify actionable solutions and explore what ICA can do to support scholars and uphold the
integrity of communication science in an increasingly contentious environment.

Katie Ellis, Curtin U, AUSTRALIA

Foundational Discussions on Gender and Communication in Latin America: Revisiting the First Meeting

Yamila Heram, U de Buenos Aires, ARGENTINA
The real history of communication research has always been “fronteriza” (border-crossing), hybrid, and
complex. However, mainstream historiographies of the field have been told from a unidimensional Global
North perspective that lacks attention to the intersections among knowers, regions, and identities. By
examining critical contributions from the Ibero-Americas, particularly in the 1970s and 1980s, the panel
advocates for a more inclusive, gender-aware, and regionally diverse history that embraces intellectual
exchanges across socio-epistemic divides.

4501 (HYBRID) ICA Sponsored: The 2025 Annual Steve Jones Internet Lecture. Casey Fiesler: “The
Internet Is Good for You. The Internet Is Bad for You.”
Saturday Sponsored Sessions
15:00–16:15
Centennial C
(Regency 3)
Moderator
Steve Jones, U of Illinois Chicago, USA
Participant
Casey Fiesler, Colorado U, USA
Hardly a week passes without a new ethical controversy centering on our lives online: privacy violations,
trolling and harassment, misinformation, negative impacts on mental health. Discussions around these
topics often come with calls for drastic technical or policy solutions, like age gating social media or even
wholesale platform bans. However, though instigating incidents make splashy headlines, the perceived
underlying problems are rarely so straightforward. Anonymity online allows harassment to flourish, but
also provides access to important support spaces, especially for stigmatized topics. Social media
recommendation algorithms can “know” us so well that it feels simultaneously invasive and validating.
Platforms can also help us find community—or push our content to the people who would hate it most.
Social media is bad for us, and social media is good for us; both of these things can be true at the same
time, and both tend to be amplified in the case of marginalized groups. This talk takes a journey through
the good and bad of people’s online experiences, from queer fan fiction writers to Black Twitter to
professional content creators to health support communities, and poses the ethical question: How can we
get less of the bad without sacrificing the good?This listing only includes educational sessions. For complete program details, including networking events, visit the
online program and/or event mobile app.

Studies show a significantly higher prevalence of mental health issues among academics compared to the
general population. This has been confirmed for communication and media scholars (see Journal of
Communication, issue 6/2024). The panel shifts the focus from diagnosis to problem-solving. Panelists
will suggest pathways to enhance individual and collective professional well-being. In addition to
discussing individual resilience, the panel gives special attention to constructive approaches to addressing
the problem on the systemic level: How can institutions and associations contribute to enhancing
professional well-being?

to current news disruptions, organizational and business challenges of journalism, technological innovation
in times of artificial intelligence, changes in formats and their consumption, the role of audiences and
professional profiles, and the value and epistemology of journalism as a social activity and as a research
field of growing interdisciplinarity. In this sense, the panel seeks to deepen and dynamize the debate on

Global South, but not the only.

4561 BLUE SKY BIG IDEAS: Poverty and Political Communication: Broadening Conceptual and

Mt. Yale

Danny Parker, Cornell U, USA

5081 LIVE FROM CALABAR, NIGERIA III: Disruptive Crackers or Neo-colonial Subservience?
Towards a Home-Grown Referencing Style for Communication Research in Africa
Sunday Regional Hub
7:00–8:15
Online Only Chairs
Itieke-Idamieba, Rivers State U, NIGERIA
Participants
Leton Kuru, Rivers State U, NIGERIA
Godswill John, U of Cross River State, NIGERIA
Ekaete George, U of Port Harcourt, NIGERIAThis listing only includes educational sessions. For complete program details, including networking events, visit the
online program and/or event mobile app.
233
The need for this discussion is borne out of a consistently observed reality over the years wherein calls for
papers in academic writings (including communication research papers and articles) are laden by a far
disproportionate majority of journals, book chapters and conference papers/seminars within the African
continent and beyond specifically mention foreign referencing styles such as the American Psychological
Association (APA), Chicago Manual of Style (CMS), Oxford, and Harvard as the preferred documentation
styles for such academic writings. For students and teachers, keeping abreast with these constantly
changing styles become confusing. Some argue that these styles are the vestiges of neo colonialism. This
panel discussion takes an in-depth look at the dynamics of the power element and structure within the
global communication firmament with a primary focus on the need to formulating a pan African
referencing/documentation style for communication research; thus, promoting and projecting the African
perspective/voice among the cacophony of academic documentation styles.

style, and genres. This panel charts these changes, aiming to account for what mediated comedy is and
what it does contemporarily.

Centennial E
(Regency 3)
Moderator
Noshir Contractor, Northwestern U, USAThis listing only includes educational sessions. For complete program details, including networking events, visit the
online program and/or event mobile app.
256
Participants
Andrea Guzman, Northern Illinois U, USA
Yingdan Lu, Northwestern U, USA
Jörg Matthes, U of Vienna, AUSTRIA
Katherine Ognyanova, Rutgers, The State U of New Jersey, USA
Taiquan Peng, Michigan State U, USA
Claes Vreese, U of Amsterdam, NETHERLANDS
This panel explores how generative AI simultaneously disrupts and consolidates communication research
practices. While AI revolutionizes research processes through automated literature reviews, data analysis,
and result interpretation and dissemination, it raises critical questions about academic merit and
knowledge production. The panel addresses how to maintain research integrity while leveraging AI
capabilities, develop ethical guidelines for AI integration, and adapt evaluation criteria for scholarly
excellence in an era where AI-assisted research becomes increasingly prevalent. Additionally, we will
discuss the development of ethical guidelines for AI use in scholarly work and the importance of
transparency in acknowledging AI contributions. Through this discussion, we aim to advance our
understanding of how communication researchers can thoughtfully integrate AI tools while preserving the
fundamental values of academic inquiry and adapting to this transformative moment in our field.

This panel has two interrelated goals. First, it seeks to identify, theorize, and interrogate terms that
elucidate the study of popular music in the digital age. Second, and equally important, the panel reveals
how popular music illuminates and problematizes the interpretation of certain commonplace concepts, in

263
Sunday Partner Panel
10:30–11:45
Quartz
(Regency 3)
Moderator
Bey-Ling Sha, Texas Tech U, USA
Participants
Amber Cox, Council of Colleges of Arts & Sciences, USA
Avery Holton, U of Utah, USA
Will Simpkins, Metropolitan State U, USA
Celia Weaver, U of Colorado Boulder, USA
From interpersonal disagreements at faculty meetings to political and military conflicts on the global stage,
there is no shortage of opportunity for leadership to demonstrate the importance of communication
practice based on proven theory. This panel of administrative and academic leaders will share theory-based
approaches to mitigating common conflicts, including the need to recruit more students even as resources
decline to serve them, to “publish or perish” even as academic journals reel from the impacts of AI, to
engage in fundraising even as public sentiment questions the value of higher education, and to find
community even as social isolation trends intensify. Come for a thoughtful conversation and leave with
concrete tips for leading communication programs in challenging times.

5361 BLUE SKY BIG IDEAS: Deliberation and Dialogue: Identifying Deliberative Interventions to
Counter the Rise of Authoritarian Populism

12:00–13:15
Mt. Yale
(Grand 3)

John Gastil, Pennsylvania State U, USA

Laura Black, Fielding Graduate U, USA

keywords of disability, disruption, and communication to put forth the following two provocations— how

disability?

As a critically inclined discipline, the field of communication cannot ignore the ongoing crisis in

5560 BLUE SKY PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT: Preventing and Managing Occupational
Intimidation of Researchers
Sunday Blue Sky Workshops
15:00–16:15
Mt. Harvard
(Grand 3)
Organizers
Nathan Matias, Cornell U, USA
Beatrys Rodrigues, Cornell U, USA
Rebekah Tromble, George Washington U, USAThis listing only includes educational sessions. For complete program details, including networking events, visit the
online program and/or event mobile app.
332
Many researchers and academic staff—particularly those from underrepresented groups in higher
education—face harassment and other occupational intimidation for their work. Yet universities have
struggled to prevent and manage intimidation, which can deter people from exercising their intellectual
freedom. In this interactive session with the Researcher Support Consortium, we will discuss lived
experiences, best practices, and research opportunities. Participants can also contribute to “In Good
Company,” a care package program for Communication scholars facing occupational intimidation.
5561 BLUE SKY BIG IDEAS: Global Exiled Journalism: What We Know and What Is Missing
Sunday Blue Sky Workshops
15:00–16:15
Mt. Yale
(Grand 3)
Organizers
Kecheng Fang, Chinese U of Hong Kong, HONG KONG
Yuting He, U of Texas at Austin, USA
Driven by rising authoritarianism, geopolitical conflicts, and advancing surveillance technologies, an
increasing number of journalists in various countries are forced into exile, making the issue of “exiled
journalism” more pressing than ever. This session brings together global scholars to explore critical
research gaps in understanding this phenomenon. It aims to identify promising research directions and
methodologies for investigating the evolving landscape of exiled journalism and its impact on democracy
and global information flows.

Cynthia Stohl’s award-winning, deeply impactful and extensive scholarship on organizational group and
technological communication is global in its scope, reach, and impact. Her work, now in its fifth decade,
has led to her becoming one of the most recognizable figures in communication studies. This panel
discusses her contributions in these domains in both serious and playful registers, focusing on her
contributions to scholarship, professional associations, and to the academy.

6000 (ONLINE ONLY) BLUE SKY PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT WORKSHOP: Scholarly
Journal Editing: Transformation and Consolidation Going Forward
Monday Blue Sky Workshops
7:00–8:15
Online Only Chairs
Sandra Braman, Michigan State U, USA
David Ewoldsen, Michigan State U, USA
Jefferson Pooley, U of Pennsylvania, USA
Journal editors curate scholarly conversations, transforming and consolidating the field as they evaluate,
select, help develop, and contextualize articles. This session is paired with the presidential panel of former
editors of ICA journals, “Editing ICA Journals: Past, Present, and Future,” refracting challenges and
opportunities through the lens of the craft of editing itself. The goal is to identify best practices for editing,
and for learning editing, in a changing technological, economic, social, and political environment. Classical
challenges facing editors of scholarly journals have historically included resource inadequacies such as not
enough time or personnel support. Semi-classical challenges arise when there are shifts in the subject
matter of the discipline (digitization, for example, is now a 60+ year old issue and is semi-classical now
rather than new), Major theoretical insights and shifts in the relative importance of particular industries also
present semi-classical problems. In the mid-2020s, challenges that are new include AI; attacks on the
credibility of science itself; and political barriers such institutional requirements for prior approval of each
communication involved in journal editing or trying to edit while living in a war zone. The session will
open with a short review of the history of scholarly journals and a brief synthesis of key points from the
presidential panel and submissions by session participants. A few individuals with experience editing key
scholarly journals not published by ICA and from the publisher’s side will open a moderated discussion
that will then broaden to the entire group. The session is open to anyone interested in thinking about
scholarly publishing through the lens of journal editing as a craft. Participants will include deeply
experienced editors, individuals new to editing, or those who wish to become an editor, and authors and
readers. The session is limited to 25 participants. Those wishing to participate should submit a short bio—This listing only includes educational sessions. For complete program details, including networking events, visit the
online program and/or event mobile app.
342
with particular reference to your own editing experience and/or aspirations—and 250–500 words on what
you see as the most pressing challenges facing editors of scholarly journals now, what they might be in
future, and what you recommend editors do to continue to move our scholarly conversation fruitfully and
usefully forward under current and future conditions. Using [ICA Blue Sky] in the subject line, please
submit to the organizers via Sandra Braman (bramansa at msu.edu) by May 15, 2025. Because the room
limit will be 25, selection of participants will ensure diversity of geographic region, subfield, theoretical
and methodological orientation, gender and sexual preference, ethnicity, race, and religion. **This is a live,
online-only encore presentation for remote attendees and hubs. The in-person version of this session is
Sunday at 1:30PM.**

to address media’s historical support of white supremacist narratives in Australia, the United Kingdom,
United States, and Canada/Turtle Island.

When the War on the Media Meets War: Anti-Media Media in Israel
Ayala Panievsky, City, U of London, UNITED KINGDOM
News can be a democratising force—or quite the opposite. This panel responds to recent calls to dedicate
greater scholarly attention to “anti-media media”: media outlets and practitioners who use the façade of
journalism to attack journalists and news organisations and undermine press freedom. Drawing on
examples from India, the US, Israel, and Hong Kong, this panel sheds light on the strategies embraced by
anti-media media in different cultural, political, and journalistic contexts, providing a timely intervention
by highlighting an increasingly consequential phenomenon.

As AI implementation speeds up in the news industries, journalism is growing increasingly reliant on a

The Tensions Between Internationalizing and Intersectionalities in the ICA
Angharad Valdivia, U of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
The scholars in this panel engage in media and communication research shaped by theoretical concepts
and paradigms outside of the communication cannon to examine the centrality of ethnicity, race,
nationality, gender, sexuality, and intersectionality to media and communication research. Collectively the
panelists explore the following questions: What do scholars gain by calling on critical literature outside of
the inter-discipline of communication? What ethical, social, and political questions does engagement with
scholarship outside of communication allow? And how does this external engagement more effectively
serve the public good, especially for communities and cultural phenomena rarely made visible in
mainstream communication research?

6501 (HYBRID) SPECIAL SESSION: U.S. Policy Climate and Far-Right Pressure Tactics: The Impact
on International Scholars and Strategies of Resistance
Monday Sponsored Sessions
15:00–16:15
Centennial C
(Regency 3)
Chair
Mohan Dutta, Massey U, U of New Zealand, NEW ZEALAND
The panel addresses the ongoing attacks on higher education in the United States with a focus on the
immediate consequences and long-term implications for communication scholarship, the academic
freedom of communication scholars, and ICA as a key player in the field. Far-right pressure tactics
mainstreamed in the current policy climate in the U.S. are particularly threatening scholarship exploring
critical questions around race, gender, ethnicity, decolonization, and whiteness. The panelists will explore
strategies of resistance to these threats and discuss adequate courses of action for individual researchers,
universities, and scholarly associations. The panel, offered in a hybrid format, is a collaboration between
the ICA Oceania Hub in Aotearoa New Zealand and the main ICA conference.

Solomon Elusoji, Georgia State U, USA

the Role of Ghanaian Agency
Richard Dwomoh, U of London, UNITED KINGDOM
The Silent Influence: China's Media Strategy and Its Impact on Journalistic Training and Narratives in

Gregory Gondwe, California State U, San Bernardino, USA
China-Africa Media Cooperation: Talking to Africa, Gazing to the West
Weidi Zheng, King’s College London, UNITED KINGDOM
Converts, Negotiators and Sceptics: Three Profiles Among Latin American Participants in Journalism
Training Programmes in China
Pablo Morales, London School of Economics & Political Science, UNITED KINGDOM
Western aid organisations have long led journalism training in the Global South, embedding democratic
and liberal media values. Recently, China has emerged as a competitor, offering training programmes for
African and Latin American journalists, for example. While critics argue these programmes promote
authoritarian values, Chinese officials claim they help journalists better understand China. Scholars like
Repnikova, Dwomoh, Gondwe, Zheng, and Morales analyse these exchanges, exploring how they might
reshape media norms and challenge Western influence.

The conference aims to provide a comprehensive discussion on protecting journalists working in conflict
zones, using the Israel-Gaza war as a case study. It seeks to address the unique challenges journalists face,
explore strategies for ensuring their safety, and highlight the role of international organizations and legal
frameworks in safeguarding press freedom during conflict. The conference will bring together experts,
journalists, and policymakers to exchange insights, share experiences, and develop actionable
recommendations to enhance the protection of journalists in war zones.
